## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 32 (*Gaṇabhojana*) governs the communal consumption of meals, laying down that a monk who eats as part of a specifically invited group of monks incurs an offense requiring confession (*pācittiya*) [SuttaCentral]. The initial formulation of the rule was remarkably terse, consisting solely of a locative phrase dependent on the offense category (*gaṇabhojane pācittiyan ti*, Vin IV 71) [Hüsken 1997]. In the course of the Vinaya narrative, the rule was amended repeatedly to accommodate various practical necessities and mitigating circumstances, such as times of famine or scarcity of food (*dubbhikkhā*) [Vinaya Pitaka vol 4; Hüsken 1997; Sujato & Brahmali 2015]. In total, the precept was modified seven times before reaching its received canonical form containing multiple explicit exceptions [Hüsken 1997; Sujato & Brahmali 2015]. 

A notable textual and philological detail occurs at Vin IV 74, where the Theravāda Vinaya reading *samaya* corresponds to *mahāsamāja* in the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Prātimokṣasūtra* (*Pāyattika* 36), illustrating historical Middle Indic phonetic developments and precanonical variations in transmission [Bechert 1991].

Curated parallels for the rule are exceptionally widespread across early Buddhist traditions [SuttaCentral]. Within the Pali canon, it corresponds directly to the rule in the *Bhikkhu Pātimokkha*, the *Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga* (Pācittiya 118), the Parivāra, and connects with the *Saṁghabhedakakkhandhaka* (Kd 17) [SuttaCentral]. Cross-sectarian parallels exist in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan recensions of the *Prātimokṣasūtra* and *Vinayavibhaṅga* belonging to the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Kāśyapīya, and Mahāsaṅghika traditions (commonly numbered as Pācittiya/Pāyattika 32, 33, 36, or 40) [SuttaCentral]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse with related food and deportment rules—notably Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 33, 57, and 46, as well as the Khandhakas (Kd 6 and Kd 1)—and aligns the text with Sanskrit and Tibetan Vinaya witnesses, including the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D0003-3), the Sanskrit *Vinayasūtra*, and the *Prātimokṣasūtraṭīkāvinayasamuccaya* (D4106-2) [DharmaNexus].
